title: The Executive Team’s Orientation Toward Risk Can Make a World of Difference in an Organization’s Performance
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Drawing on Halvorson and Higgins's book Focus, the post contrasts two leadership orientations: a promotion focus on growth and gain, and a preservation focus on security and loss avoidance. Either can be right depending on context. The author reports that organizations led by opportunity-focused senior leaders tend to outperform preservation-focused ones, linking this to transformational leadership and to greater creativity and adaptability. The post does not dismiss vigilance and suggests pairing the two, placing preservation-minded leaders in protective roles so senior leaders can chase possibility. It ends with diagnostic questions about which orientation drives your top team.
points: Leaders differ in whether they are energized by what could be gained or by what must be protected.
Emerging research ties opportunity-focused leadership to transformational behaviors and to organizational creativity and adaptability.
Preservation focus is still valued, especially in moments of peril and in roles that guard what has been earned.
The suggested design is to put preservation-minded leaders in protective functions so senior leaders are free to pursue opportunity.
The warning is against letting a default of caution make the most consequential decisions.
quotes: Of the many differences in approach, mindset, and strategic focus that separate leaders, perhaps none is more impactful than how they view risk and opportunity. In their landmark book Focus, psychologists Heidi Grant Halvorson and Tory Higgins make the case that leaders and people operate from one of two distinct orientations.
The orientation is driven by the pursuit of advancement, growth, and gain. Leaders who operate this way are energized by what could be achieved.
Leaders with a preservation focus are energized by what must be protected. They move carefully, remain vigilant, attend to risk, and are most engaged when they sense something important is at stake.

That said, emerging data suggest that organizations with senior leaders who maintain an opportunity focus generally outperform those whose senior leaders focus on preservation and stability. The research helps to explain why this performance advantage exists.

Studies consistently link opportunity-focused leadership to transformational leadership behaviors, while prevention-focused leadership tends to manifest as transactional leadership. This distinction matters enormously at the organizational level.

Good organizations cultivate both, deploying leaders with a preservation focus in functions and in roles where protecting what has been earned is critical. This frees senior leaders to unleash their opportunity focus on what is possible.

What leaders cannot do, according to the research on high-performing organizations, is to allow a default orientation toward caution and loss avoidance to dictate their most consequential decisions. In a world that now clearly rewards those who move toward opportunity, the greatest risk of all may be not taking enough of it.
